CKD manifestations include symptoms and clinical/laboratory abnormalities associated with CKD, which confer health implications. Rationale There are limited data in CKD populations on the risks and beneﬁts of physical activity interventions. The quality of evi- dence is low or very low. Nonetheless, short-term studies suggest that physical activity interventions lower BP, decrease weight, and improve the mental aspects of quality of life. These data are consistent with a substantial body of evidence demonstrating that physical activity improves BP, dysglycemia, cardiopulmonary ﬁtness, physical function, and mood in the general population. Prevalence of hypertension and diabetes, and risk of CV disease are extremely high in CKD populations, suggesting that the absolute beneﬁt of physical activity in- terventions may be enhanced in CKD if the relative beneﬁts are equivalent to those observed in the general population. text: Screening for albuminuria can be most easily performed by urine albumin-to- creatinine ratio (UACR) in a random spot urine collection (1). Timed or 24-h collec­ tions are more burdensome, and in many clinical scenarios it is preferable to mea­ sure UACR. text: A regular exercise routine can help people with kidney disease feel better and support related conditions like high blood pressure, blood sugar, and heart health. Making activity a regular part of the week helps build strength and energy and makes everyday tasks easier.
title: National Kidney Foundation - Exercise and Chronic Kidney Disease (patient education)

text: Regular activity can support better blood pressure, lower the risk of developing diabetes, improve blood sugar for people who already have diabetes, build muscle strength, help with a healthy weight, and improve mood by easing anxiety and low feelings.
title: National Kidney Foundation - Exercise and Chronic Kidney Disease (patient education)

text: Helpful activity can include aerobic movement such as walking, and gentle strength work using light weights or resistance bands to support muscles and bones. Choosing activities a person enjoys makes a routine easier to keep.
title: National Kidney Foundation - Exercise and Chronic Kidney Disease (patient education)

text: Long periods of sitting or bed rest reduce muscle strength over time, so gentle, regular movement matters. It is best to start at a comfortable level and build up slowly, increasing how long and how often a person is active as they feel able.
title: National Kidney Foundation - Exercise and Chronic Kidney Disease (patient education)

text: Before starting a new exercise routine, it is a good idea to talk with a clinician about what is safe. Warming up, using suitable footwear, not holding the breath during effort, and stopping if something does not feel right all help keep activity safe.
title: National Kidney Foundation - Exercise and Chronic Kidney Disease (patient education)

text: Having more muscle makes it easier to keep a healthy weight, which is better for kidney health. Building activity into a regular daily or weekly routine helps it become a lasting habit.
title: National Kidney Foundation - Exercise and Chronic Kidney Disease (patient education)

text: CKD risk factors Approximately 1 in 3 adults with diabetes and 1 of 5 adults with high blood pressure may have CKD. Other problems that put you at greater chance of kidney disease include: Heart disease. High blood pressure. Overweight or obesity. Family history of CKD. Kidney infections and a physical injury can also cause kidney disease. People who have diabetes may be able to prevent or delay CKD with blood pressure-lowering drugs. These medicines reduce protein in the urine, a risk factor for developing CKD. Having CKD increases the chances of heart disease and stroke. text: Risk Factors for Chronic Kidney Disease KEY POINTS Approximately 1 in 3 adults with diabetes has chronic kidney disease (CKD). About 1 in 5 adults with high blood pressure has CKD. Adults with heart failure also have a higher risk of CKD. Risk factors Diabetes CKD is common in people with diabetes. Approximately 1 in 3 adults with diabetes has CKD. Each kidney is made up of millions of tiny filters called nephrons. High blood sugar from diabetes can damage blood vessels in the kidneys and nephrons so they don't work well. High blood pressure Approximately 1 in 5 adults with high blood pressure has CKD. High blood pressure can make blood vessels narrower, reducing blood flow. Over time, blood vessels throughout the body weaken, including in the kidneys. Damaged blood vessels in the kidneys may no longer work properly.
